58923.etyen:
From syer (“person who sews professionally”) + -ske (“feminine occupational suffix”).
The base syer (“person who sews professionally”) is formed from sy (“to sew”) + -er (“agent noun suffix”), with sy (“to sew”) from Old Norse sýja (“to sew”). The suffix -ske (“feminine occupational suffix”) is from Middle Low German -sche, the feminine substantivized form of adjectival -sch, corresponding to Norwegian -sk. It was subsequently blended with the feminine suffix -se, from Old French -esse (“feminine noun suffix”).
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk syerske and Danish syerske (“seamstress, dressmaker”).

25387.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse há (“aftergrass”), from Proto-Norse ᚺᚨᚺᚨ (haha, “aftergrass”), from Proto-Germanic *hah(w)ō (“aftergrass”).
Compare Icelandic há (“aftergrass”), Norwegian Nynorsk hå (“aftergrass”) and Faroese hógvur (“remaining stubble of cut grass”). / Inherited from Old Norse hár (“spiny dogfish”). The further origin is uncertain. De Vries connects the Old Norse word with an earlier form related to *hōhô (“plow”), perhaps with reference to the jagged form of a shark; another proposal compares *hawwaną (“to hew, cut”).
The same Old Norse word was borrowed as Middle Dutch haeye (“shark”), whence Dutch haai (“shark”); Bokmål later borrowed the Dutch word as hai (“shark”). Doublet of hai (“shark”).
Compare Icelandic hár (“dogfish”), Faroese Faroese háur and hávur (“shark”), and Norwegian Nynorsk hå (“spiny dogfish”).

1000235.etyen:
Internationalism, based on Latin Venus (“Venus, the Roman goddess; the planet Venus”), from the common noun Latin venus (“loveliness, beauty, charm”), from Proto-Indo-European *wénh₁-os (“loveliness”), from the root *wenh₁- (“to wish, love”).
The astronomical sense is transferred from the name of the Roman goddess. The use as a female given name is likewise ultimately based on the mythological name.
